title: Open Field Test Analysis of Animal Movement
author: Tomokazu Konishi
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bhc8j2zw

steps.title: Prepare open‑field arena
steps.instruction: Use plastic container boxes (available at DIY stores) as the open‑field arena; choose box colors that give high contrast with the animal, optionally color or spot a specific animal part, and ensure the animal’s shape can be separated from the background in black‑and‑white images.

steps.title: Set up video recording
steps.instruction: Mount any small digital or movie camera on a tripod directly above the arena, point it straight down, and start recording before placing the animal so that empty frames are captured for background subtraction; no extra illumination is required, and the camera must be able to save in a format that can be converted to .avi. Use at least the minimum resolution needed (≈150 × 150 px is sufficient for a 50 × 50 cm field).

substeps.instruction: Fix the camera with a tripod and aim it from straight above.
Start recording before the animal is introduced to obtain vacant background frames.
Do not add extra lighting; uneven illumination will be compensated later using the background frames.

steps.title: Convert video to .avi if needed
steps.instruction: If the camera records in a non‑avi format, convert the file to .avi using freeware such as XMediaRecord; during conversion you may crop the frame and reduce the resolution (≈150 × 150 px is adequate).

steps.title: Import video into ImageJ
steps.instruction: Drag‑and‑drop the .avi file into ImageJ (referred to as “the Image”), open it as a grayscale stack to reduce file size, and enable the stack option; note that a 30‑minute movie will generate roughly 54 000 frames, requiring a PC with ample RAM.

steps.title: Duplicate image stack
steps.instruction: In ImageJ choose Image → Duplicate and select “duplicate stack” to create a copy that can be altered without affecting the original.

steps.title: Invert brightness (optional)
steps.instruction: If the animal appears black on a white background, apply Edit → Invert to facilitate background subtraction.

steps.title: Binarize frames
steps.instruction: Convert each frame to black‑and‑white by selecting Image → Adjust → Threshold, which simplifies the grayscale tone to a binary image emphasizing animal edges.

steps.title: Measure position and area
steps.instruction: Open Analyze → Set Measurements, check “Area”, “Center of mass”, and “Display label”; then run Analyze → Analyze Particles to obtain the animal’s position and area for each frame, and save the “Results” as a tab‑separated text file (e.g., via Excel).

steps.title: Analyze data in R
steps.instruction: Import the tab‑separated results file into R; run the R script provided in the appendix to compute movement parameters using several constant distribution patterns, performing any required manual tuning as indicated in the script comments.
